names.official: Federal personal income tax (Income Tax Act, Part I)
names.native: Impôt fédéral sur le revenu des particuliers

taxes.base: Taxable income of individuals resident in Canada (worldwide income), and of non-residents on Canadian employment, business and certain capital-gains income.
taxes.payer: Individuals; employers withhold at source through payroll deductions.

rate.headline: 14% – 33% (five brackets, 2026)
details: 14% on the first $58,523 of taxable income
The lowest rate fell from 15% to 14% on 1 July 2025 (14.5% blended for the 2025 tax year); thresholds indexed 2.0% for 2026.

instruments.explanation: The largest federal revenue source. Income is taxed in brackets; credits such as the basic personal amount reduce tax. Provinces and territories add their own income tax on top (see the provincial level).
exceptions: Residents of Québec receive a 16.5% federal abatement of basic federal tax because Québec runs its own income-tax system.
Provincial and territorial income taxes are levied separately, so combined marginal rates differ by province.

legalRefs.locator: s. 117(2) (tax payable by individuals – rates and brackets)
Federal brackets for the 2026 tax year

names.official: Federal corporate income tax (Income Tax Act, Part I)
names.native: Impôt fédéral sur le revenu des sociétés

taxes.base: Taxable income of corporations resident in Canada and Canadian-source business income of non-resident corporations.

rate.headline: 15% general; 9% small-business rate
details: Basic rate 38%, reduced to 28% by the provincial abatement and to 15% by the general rate reduction.
Canadian-controlled private corporations pay 9% on active business income up to the $500,000 business limit (small business deduction).

instruments.explanation: A flat federal rate applied to corporate taxable income, with a reduced rate for small Canadian-controlled private corporations. Provinces and territories levy their own corporate tax on top.
exceptions: Special rates and credits apply to manufacturing, investment income of private corporations, and certain resource activities.
Combined federal-provincial rates differ by province.

legalRefs.locator: s. 123 (rate), s. 123.4 (general rate reduction), s. 125 (small business deduction)

names.official: Tax on income from Canada of non-residents (Income Tax Act, Part XIII)
names.native: Impôt des non-résidents (partie XIII)

taxes.base: Certain Canadian-source income paid to non-residents: dividends, most rents and royalties, pensions, some interest.
taxes.payer: Non-resident recipients; the Canadian payer withholds and remits.

rate.headline: 25% statutory; reduced by tax treaties
details: Statutory rate is 25% of the gross amount.
Tax treaties commonly lower the rate on dividends, interest and royalties; most arm's-length interest is exempt.

instruments.explanation: A withholding tax collected at source on income flowing to foreign residents, so that Canada taxes the return on Canadian assets held abroad.
exceptions: The rate you actually face depends on your country's tax treaty with Canada and on the type of income.

legalRefs.locator: Part XIII, s. 212 (25% tax on income payable to non-residents)

names.official: Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax – federal component (Excise Tax Act, Part IX)
names.native: Taxe sur les produits et services (TPS) / taxe de vente harmonisée (TVH)

taxes.base: Most supplies of goods and services made in Canada and imports, as a value-added tax with input tax credits.
taxes.payer: Borne by final consumers; registered businesses collect and remit it.

rate.headline: 5% GST; HST 13%–15% in participating provinces
details: 5% GST applies nationally.
HST (5% federal + provincial part): Ontario 13%; Nova Scotia 14% (from 1 Apr 2025); New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island 15%.
British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba charge a separate PST; Québec charges the QST; Alberta and the territories charge no provincial sales tax.

instruments.explanation: A broad consumption tax. The federal government collects the HST in participating provinces and passes the provincial part to the province; only the federal part counts as federal revenue.
exceptions: Zero-rated: basic groceries, prescription drugs, exports. Exempt: most health, education and financial services.
Revenu Québec administers the GST in Québec on the federal government's behalf.

instruments.statusNote: Temporarily suspended since 20 April 2026 (enacted by Bill C-30 to 7 Sep 2026); an extension to 31 Jan 2027 with 50% rates until 31 Mar 2027 was announced 2 Sep 2026 and was still at the legislative-proposal stage when checked.

names.official: Excise tax on gasoline, diesel fuel and aviation fuels (Excise Tax Act, Part III)
names.native: Taxe d'accise sur l'essence, le carburant diesel et les carburants d'aviation

taxes.base: Litres of gasoline, diesel and aviation fuels delivered or imported.
taxes.payer: Fuel producers and importers; passed on in pump prices.

rate.headline: Statutory 10¢/L gasoline, 4¢/L diesel – currently suspended (0¢/L)
details: Statutory rates: 10¢/L gasoline and unleaded aviation gasoline; 11¢/L leaded aviation gasoline; 4¢/L diesel and aviation fuel other than aviation gasoline.
Suspended (0¢/L) since 20 April 2026.
Announced schedule: 0¢ until 31 Jan 2027; 50% of statutory rates 1 Feb – 31 Mar 2027; full rates from 1 Apr 2027 (extension not yet enacted at the date checked).

instruments.explanation: A per-litre excise on transportation fuels. In 2026 the government temporarily set it to zero as an affordability measure; the revenue shown is the last full fiscal year before the suspension.
exceptions: Provinces levy their own separate fuel taxes; this federal excise is unaffected by them.

legalRefs.locator: Part III, s. 23 (excise tax on gasoline, diesel fuel and aviation fuels)

names.official: Excise duties on alcohol, tobacco and cannabis products (Excise Act, 2001)
names.native: Droits d'accise sur l'alcool, le tabac et le cannabis

taxes.base: Production/packaging of spirits, wine, beer, tobacco and cannabis products.
taxes.payer: Licensed producers and packagers; passed on to consumers.

rate.headline: Per-unit rates set in the Excise Act, 2001
details: Rates are specific (per litre of absolute ethyl alcohol, per cigarette, per gram of cannabis product).
Alcohol duty rates are adjusted each 1 April; the inflation-linked increase is capped at 2% per year under measures confirmed with Bill C-30 (2026).

instruments.explanation: Duties charged when alcohol, tobacco or cannabis products are produced or packaged, in addition to GST/HST and provincial taxes.
exceptions: Reduced alcohol duty rates apply to the first part of small brewers' production.

names.official: Air Travellers Security Charge
names.native: Droit pour la sécurité des passagers du transport aérien

taxes.base: Each chargeable enplanement on commercial air travel.

rate.headline: $9.46–$9.94 domestic; $16.08–$16.89 transborder; $34.42 international
details: Domestic: $9.46 per enplanement with GST/HST, $9.94 without (max $18.92 / $19.87 per one-way itinerary).
Transborder (USA): $16.08 with GST/HST, $16.89 without (max $32.16 / $33.77).
Other international: flat $34.42.
Rates in force since 1 May 2024.

instruments.explanation: A per-flight charge earmarked in policy to fund air-travel security, reported by the government within tax revenues.
exceptions: Exemptions exist for certain diplomats, crew, infants under two, and some remote flights.

names.official: Customs import duties (Customs Tariff; Customs Act)
names.native: Droits de douane à l'importation

taxes.base: Value (or quantity) of imported goods by tariff classification and origin.

rate.headline: Schedule of rates by tariff item; many goods duty-free
details: Rates are set line-by-line in the Customs Tariff; preferential or zero rates apply under trade agreements such as CUSMA.
Temporary surtaxes imposed by order under the Customs Tariff (for example counter-measures on some U.S. and Chinese goods) change frequently; check the CBSA tariff pages for current orders.

instruments.explanation: Duties collected at the border by the Canada Border Services Agency. Revenue rose in 2025 as counter-tariff surtaxes were introduced; the amount shown is FY2024-25 and only partly reflects them.
exceptions: Origin rules, remission orders and free-trade agreements can reduce or eliminate duty.

names.official: Employment Insurance premiums
names.native: Cotisations d'assurance-emploi

taxes.base: Insurable earnings of employees up to the annual maximum ($68,900 in 2026).
taxes.payer: Employees and employers (employer pays 1.4 times the employee premium).

rate.headline: 1.63% employee; 2.282% employer (2026)
details: Maximum insurable earnings $68,900; maximum employee premium $1,123.07, employer $1,572.30.
Québec: 1.30% employee (2026), because the Québec Parental Insurance Plan covers maternity and parental benefits.

instruments.explanation: An insurance premium, not a general tax: payments fund EI benefits for insured workers who lose work or take leave. Premiums are recorded in federal revenues.
exceptions: Self-employed people may opt in to some EI special benefits.
Québec residents pay reduced EI premiums and separate QPIP premiums.

instruments.statusNote: Enacted reduction of the base CPP rate from 9.9% to 9.5% (4.95% to 4.75% each side) effective 1 January 2027 (Bill C-30, Royal Assent 18 June 2026).

names.official: Canada Pension Plan contributions
names.native: Cotisations au Régime de pensions du Canada

taxes.base: Pensionable earnings between the basic exemption ($3,500) and the annual maximum ($74,600 in 2026), plus second-tier CPP2 earnings up to $85,000.
taxes.payer: Employees and employers equally; the self-employed pay both shares.

rate.headline: 5.95% each on base+first additional; 4% each on CPP2 (2026)
details: 2026: 5.95% employee and 5.95% employer on earnings between $3,500 and $74,600 (maximum $4,230.45 each).
CPP2: 4% employee and 4% employer on earnings from $74,600 to $85,000 (maximum $416.00 each).
Scheduled: base rate falls from 9.9% to 9.5% combined (4.75% each) from 1 January 2027.

instruments.explanation: A social-insurance contribution that funds the earnings-related retirement, disability and survivor benefits of the Canada Pension Plan. It sits outside the federal government's budgetary revenues and is invested by CPP Investments.
exceptions: Québec has its own Québec Pension Plan (QPP) with separate contributions administered by Retraite Québec; CPP does not apply to Québec employment.

legalRefs.locator: Division on the base CPP contribution rate

instruments.statusNote: Repealed in effect: all fuel-charge rates were set to zero from 1 April 2025. The revenue shown is for FY2024-25, when the charge was still collected.

names.official: Fuel charge (Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act, Part 1)
names.native: Redevance sur les combustibles

taxes.base: Delivery, import or use of fossil fuels in listed provinces, by carbon content.
taxes.payer: Fuel distributors and importers; passed on to consumers.

rate.headline: $0 since 1 April 2025 (was $80/tonne CO₂e in 2024-25)
details: Regulations set all fuel-charge rates to zero after 31 March 2025.
The government has proposed repealing the fuel-charge framework in phases; the requirement for provinces to have a consumer carbon price has also ended.

instruments.explanation: The federal consumer carbon price. Proceeds were returned mainly through the Canada Carbon Rebate. It no longer raises revenue, but FY2024-25 revenue is shown because it was the last year of collection.
exceptions: Industrial carbon pricing (output-based pricing systems) is a separate mechanism that continues.

names.official: Provincial and territorial personal income taxes
names.native: Impôts provinciaux et territoriaux sur le revenu des particuliers

taxes.base: Taxable income of individuals resident in the province or territory on 31 December.

rate.headline: Varies by jurisdiction – each sets its own brackets
details: Ten provinces and three territories each set their own progressive brackets, rates and credits.
Outside Québec the CRA collects provincial income tax on the same return as federal tax; Québec residents file a separate Québec return with Revenu Québec.

instruments.explanation: Provincial income taxes are levied on top of federal income tax and are a main source of provincial revenue.
exceptions: No single national rate exists – see each province's or territory's schedule of brackets.

legalRefs.locator: Provincial and territorial rates are listed alongside the federal table

names.official: Provincial and territorial corporate income taxes
names.native: Impôts provinciaux et territoriaux sur le revenu des sociétés

taxes.base: Taxable income of corporations earned through a permanent establishment in the province or territory.

rate.headline: Varies by jurisdiction – general rate and lower small-business rate
details: Every jurisdiction has a general rate and a lower rate for income eligible for the federal small business deduction.
Québec and Alberta administer their own corporate income tax; the CRA collects it for the other provinces and the territories.

instruments.explanation: A second layer of corporate income tax that adds to the 15% federal rate.
exceptions: Rates and thresholds change often; see the CRA table or each province's finance ministry.

names.official: Provincial sales taxes: PST, Québec sales tax (QST) and the provincial part of the HST
names.native: Taxes de vente provinciales (TVP, TVQ, part provinciale de la TVH)

taxes.base: Retail sales and services (PST) or most supplies (QST, HST) in the province.
taxes.payer: Final consumers; businesses collect and remit.

rate.headline: Varies: BC 7%, SK 6%, MB 7%, QC 9.975% QST, HST provincial part 8–10%
details: Retail PST: British Columbia 7%, Saskatchewan 6%, Manitoba 7%.
Québec Sales Tax (QST): 9.975%, a value-added tax administered by Revenu Québec.
Provincial part of the HST: Ontario 8%, Nova Scotia 9%, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island 10%.
Alberta and the three territories levy no general sales tax.

instruments.explanation: Provincial consumption taxes that sit on top of the 5% GST. The largest single category of provincial 'general taxes on goods and services'.
exceptions: Base and exemptions differ: PSTs tax fewer items than the HST/QST, and rebates and exemptions vary by province.

names.official: Provincial employer payroll taxes (health and post-secondary levies)
names.native: Taxes provinciales sur la masse salariale

taxes.base: Employers' total remuneration paid to employees (above an exemption in some provinces).

rate.headline: Varies by jurisdiction – set by each province
details: Examples: Ontario Employer Health Tax, Québec Health Services Fund contributions, British Columbia Employer Health Tax, Manitoba's Health and Post-Secondary Education Tax Levy.
Exemption thresholds and rate scales differ; several provinces have none.

instruments.explanation: Taxes on payrolls used to fund health and education spending. They are separate from EI premiums and CPP contributions.
exceptions: Not levied in every province; small employers are often exempt.

names.official: Provincial property-related taxes (provincial property taxes and land transfer taxes)
names.native: Taxes provinciales sur la propriété et les transferts immobiliers

taxes.base: Assessed property value (education property tax where the province levies it) and the value of land transfers (land transfer tax where levied).

rate.headline: Varies by jurisdiction – no national rate
details: Some provinces levy provincial or education property taxes (e.g. Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta); others do not.
Land transfer taxes are provincial in Ontario, British Columbia (property transfer tax), Manitoba and some others; in Québec and Nova Scotia they are municipal.

instruments.explanation: Statistics Canada groups provincial property taxes and transfer taxes in one category, so the two cannot be separated in the aggregate figure.
exceptions: Rebates, first-time-buyer relief and property classes differ across provinces.

names.official: Provincial gasoline and motive fuel taxes
names.native: Taxes provinciales sur les carburants

taxes.base: Litres of gasoline, diesel and other motive fuels sold in the province.

rate.headline: Varies by jurisdiction – cents per litre
details: Each province sets its own per-litre rate, often different for gasoline and diesel and for regions within the province.
British Columbia's consumer carbon tax and the federal consumer fuel charge were both removed in April 2025.

instruments.explanation: Per-litre taxes on road fuels that add to the federal excise tax and GST/HST.
exceptions: Rates change with budgets; several provinces have temporarily cut fuel taxes.

names.official: Provincial tobacco, cannabis and liquor taxes
names.native: Taxes provinciales sur le tabac, le cannabis et les alcools

taxes.base: Tobacco products, cannabis products and (in some provinces) alcoholic beverages.
taxes.payer: Consumers, collected from wholesalers and retailers.

rate.headline: Varies by jurisdiction
details: Tobacco taxes are per-cigarette or ad valorem and differ by province.
Alcohol is mainly raised through provincial liquor-board mark-ups, which are profits rather than taxes and are excluded here.

instruments.explanation: Excise-style taxes that supplement the federal excise duties.
exceptions: Statistics Canada reports liquor taxes separately from liquor-board profits.

names.official: Provincial natural resource royalties (oil and gas, minerals, forestry, water power)
names.native: Redevances provinciales sur les ressources naturelles

taxes.base: Extraction of provincially owned oil, gas, minerals, timber and water power.

rate.headline: Varies by jurisdiction and resource
details: Each province sets its own royalty regime by resource (e.g. price-sensitive oil and gas royalties in Alberta).
Royalties are payments for use of publicly owned resources, not taxes.

instruments.explanation: Provinces own the resources within their borders, so resource rent flows to them as royalties rather than through the federal tax system.
exceptions: Royalty formulas change with commodity prices and policy.

legalRefs.locator: s. 109 (ownership of lands, mines, minerals and royalties); s. 92A

names.official: Workers' compensation premiums (assessments)
names.native: Cotisations aux commissions des accidents du travail

taxes.base: Employers' insured payroll, by industry risk class.

rate.headline: Varies by jurisdiction and industry class
details: Each provincial and territorial workers' compensation board sets average and class-specific assessment rates annually.

instruments.explanation: Insurance premiums that fund no-fault cover for workplace injuries. They are compulsory but are not general taxes.
exceptions: Some occupations and small employers are excluded in certain provinces.

names.official: Municipal property taxes (real property taxes, business property taxes and payments in lieu)
names.native: Taxes foncières municipales

taxes.base: Assessed value of land and buildings (real property), with classes such as residential, commercial and industrial.

rate.headline: Varies by municipality – mill rate set annually
details: Each council sets a rate (tax per $1,000 of assessed value, or a percentage) by property class within limits set by the province.
Payments in lieu of taxes are made by governments on exempt properties.

instruments.explanation: The backbone of Canadian municipal finance. Assessment is often done by a provincial agency (for example MPAC in Ontario) while the municipality sets the rate.
exceptions: Education portions collected with the property tax bill may be remitted to school boards or the province; they can be classified differently.

legalRefs.locator: Ontario example – provisions on municipal taxation

names.official: Municipal land transfer taxes (e.g. Toronto Municipal Land Transfer Tax; Québec transfer duties)
names.native: Droits de mutation immobilière

taxes.base: Value of consideration for the transfer of real property.

rate.headline: Varies – only some municipalities may levy it
details: Authorised for the City of Toronto (Municipal Land Transfer Tax), Québec municipalities (transfer duties) and Nova Scotia municipalities (deed transfer tax); other municipalities cannot.

instruments.explanation: A one-time tax when property changes hands, charged in addition to any provincial tax.
exceptions: Not available to most Canadian municipalities.

legalRefs.locator: Toronto example – municipal land transfer tax provisions

names.official: Development charges and offsite levies
names.native: Redevances d'aménagement

taxes.base: New development and redevelopment, to pay for growth-related infrastructure.
taxes.payer: Developers and builders, passed on in prices.

rate.headline: Varies by municipality and type of development
details: Set by municipal by-law under provincial enabling legislation (for example Ontario's Development Charges Act, 1997); some provinces restrict or legislate exemptions and discounts.

instruments.explanation: Charges earmarked for capital works such as water, roads and transit that serve new development.
exceptions: Recent provincial reforms in several provinces have capped, discounted or exempted some charges.

names.official: Municipal user fees, utility charges and sales of goods and services
names.native: Tarifs et frais d'utilisation municipaux

taxes.base: Use of municipal services such as water and wastewater, waste collection, transit fares, recreation and permits.

rate.headline: Varies by municipality and service
details: Fee schedules are set by by-law and usually intended to recover the cost of a service.

instruments.explanation: Charges for specific services, not taxes. Together with property tax they are the biggest own-source revenues of municipalities.
exceptions: Water and transit may be run by separate municipal corporations whose revenue is classified elsewhere.

legalRefs.locator: Ontario example – fees and charges provisions

names.official: Municipal licences, permits and charges for permission to use goods or perform activities
names.native: Permis et licences municipaux

taxes.base: Business licences, building permits, dog licences and similar authorisations.

rate.headline: Varies by municipality and permit type
details: Fees are set by by-law.

instruments.explanation: Statistics Canada classes permission charges as 'taxes on use of goods and on permission to use goods or perform activities', though most are fee-like.
exceptions: Building-permit fees are supposed to be limited to the cost of administering the building code in several provinces.

names.official: Municipal accommodation taxes and other taxes on specific services
names.native: Taxe sur l'hébergement et autres taxes sur des services

taxes.base: Short-term stays in hotels and rentals, and other specific services.

rate.headline: Varies – typically a few percent of the room rate
details: Authorised by provincial law in some provinces (for example Ontario's municipal accommodation tax, Toronto's City of Toronto Act, 2006); the rate, base and exemptions differ.

instruments.explanation: A small local tax that funds tourism or general municipal services where the province allows it.
exceptions: Not every municipality may levy it.

legalRefs.locator: Toronto example – municipal accommodation tax authority
